Description: A gypsum alabaster wall relief, about 3.30 meters high, from facade L of the palace of Sargon II (722-705 BC) at Dur-Sharrukin (Khorsabad), excavated by Paul-Emile Botta in 1843-1844 and now in the Louvre (AO 19873-74). It shows Sargon, recognizable by his truncated-cone royal headdress, holding the staff of kingship as he welcomes a high official - identified by the Louvre as possibly Sennacherib, the crown prince, and by some as his marshal, the tartan.
Interpretations: The relief visualizes the Assyrian court at the height of Sargon's power, the generation that ended the northern kingdom. Its staff in the king's hand echoes Isaiah's image of Assyria as the 'rod' and 'staff' of God's anger, and Sargon is the one Assyrian king named in the Bible (Isaiah 20:1). The dignitary's identity - crown prince Sennacherib or the tartan - is not settled, and the relief should not be captioned as a portrait of either man without that qualification.
AlternativeNames: Sargon II and a High Official
BiblicalSignificance: It shows the king who destroyed Samaria and the court that sent the tartan to Ashdod, the only Assyrian king the Bible names, in the regalia of his office.
DiscoveryLocation: Khorsabad, Iraq (Dur-Sharrukin, palace of Sargon II)
